how-the-internet-works.description: Your phone sends a request through Wi-Fi and the internet to a restaurant-order API. The server returns order status.
steps: Tap “Place order” — the browser creates an HTTPS request.
Your router and ISP carry packets toward the service.
A server processes the request and persists the order.
The response travels back and the UI shows the order ID.
how-the-internet-works.engineering: Network hops can fail independently; use timeouts, TLS, and request IDs when building Spring Boot APIs.

dns-explained.description: A browser must translate a domain name into an IP address before reaching the server.
steps: The browser checks its cached DNS entry.
On a miss, a recursive resolver looks up the name.
Authoritative DNS returns the current record and TTL.
The browser connects to the resolved IP.
dns-explained.engineering: DNS caches are TTL-bound; plan for stale records and connection reuse during deployments.

http-https.example: Logging in to an ecommerce store
http-https.description: The browser establishes an encrypted connection before submitting credentials.
steps: The browser requests a secure connection.
TLS establishes encryption and authenticates the server certificate.
An HTTP request carries the login payload over TLS.
The API returns a status and secure session token or cookie.
http-https.engineering: Use HTTPS everywhere, validate tokens, and never log passwords or bearer tokens.

load-balancer-algorithms.description: A load balancer spreads many checkout requests across healthy replicas.
steps: Requests arrive at a public endpoint.
The load balancer selects a healthy backend.
Different requests can reach different instances.
Health checks remove failed instances from rotation.
load-balancer-algorithms.engineering: Round robin ignores unequal request cost; consider least-connections and autoscaling.

consistent-hashing.description: Adding one cache server should not shuffle almost every cached product key.
steps: Hash the product ID into a stable numeric position.
Walk clockwise on the ring to the next node.
Read or write the key on its owning node.
When membership changes, only some keys gain a new owner.
consistent-hashing.engineering: Virtual nodes improve balancing; immutable ring snapshots are helpful for thread-safe routing.

cache-aside.description: The first product request reads PostgreSQL; subsequent requests hit Redis.
steps: The API checks Redis using a product key.
A miss falls through to the database.
The API stores the result with a TTL.
The next request can read the cached value.
cache-aside.engineering: Avoid stampedes using single-flight locks; invalidation and stale prices require care.

cdn-and-ttl.description: Static files are served from an edge location, then refreshed after their cache lifetime.
steps: A viewer requests the thumbnail from a nearby edge.
A cache hit returns it without contacting origin.
Once TTL expires, the edge revalidates with origin.
The refreshed asset is cached for later viewers.
cdn-and-ttl.engineering: Use hashed asset filenames for safe long-lived caching and explicit invalidation when needed.

sql-vs-nosql.description: Transactions require strong relational constraints, while a flexible catalog can use document records.
steps: Identify access patterns and invariants.
Choose relational tables for transactional order integrity.
Choose documents when nested product attributes vary.
Test indexing, queries, and consistency needs under load.
sql-vs-nosql.engineering: Choose by correctness and access patterns, not popularity; Hibernate/JPA and reactive stores differ.

indexing.example: Finding an order by order number
indexing.description: A database index avoids scanning every row to locate one order.
steps: An API requests order_no = 2031.
The database planner chooses an index when beneficial.
The index narrows the row locations.
The database fetches matching data and returns it.
indexing.engineering: Indexes speed reads but increase write amplification; inspect EXPLAIN plans before optimizing.

sharding-and-replication.description: Partition orders by tenant ID and replicate each partition for availability.
steps: A tenant ID is hashed or mapped to a shard.
The router directs writes to the owning primary.
The primary commits the order locally.
Replication sends changes to another copy.
sharding-and-replication.engineering: Rebalancing and replication lag are major concerns; choose shard keys by traffic distribution.

kafka-fundamentals.description: An API publishes a compliance event; consumers in a group process records from partitions.
steps: A Spring Boot producer publishes an event with a key.
Kafka appends it to an assigned partition.
One consumer in a group receives that partition.
The consumer processes and commits its offset.
kafka-fundamentals.engineering: Kafka is commonly at-least-once; handle duplicates with idempotent processing and stable event IDs.

queues-vs-events.description: A work queue distributes invoice jobs; an event stream lets multiple teams independently react.
steps: An order is marked paid.
A queue sends a work item to an invoice worker.
An event stream can broadcast the order-paid fact to many services.
Consumers acknowledge work or track offsets independently.
queues-vs-events.engineering: Queues distribute tasks; streams retain ordered histories within partitions and enable replay.

rate-limiting.description: A token bucket permits bursts while blocking repeated abusive requests.
steps: A user makes a login-code request.
The limiter checks available tokens for the identity.
If a token exists, the call proceeds.
If exhausted, return HTTP 429 and a retry hint.
rate-limiting.engineering: For distributed Spring Boot replicas, Redis atomics or gateway limits avoid per-instance bypass.

retries-circuit-breakers.description: Retries can recover transient faults, but a circuit breaker stops hammering a failing dependency.
steps: A downstream call times out.
A bounded retry adds jitter and backoff.
Repeated failure opens the breaker.
New requests fail fast until a probe confirms recovery.
retries-circuit-breakers.engineering: Only retry safe/idempotent operations; set deadlines and use Resilience4j with clear metrics.

cap-and-consistency.example: Updating an account balance during a network split
cap-and-consistency.description: When two replicas lose contact, the system must choose how to handle operations that need cross-replica agreement.
steps: A client submits an update to replica A.
Connectivity between replicas is disrupted.
A consistency-first system may reject writes lacking quorum.
An availability-first system may accept divergent writes and reconcile later.
cap-and-consistency.engineering: CAP describes behavior under partitions, not a blanket tradeoff for every normal request.

leader-election.example: One scheduled billing job across replicas
leader-election.description: Only one instance should coordinate a shared scheduled task at a time.
steps: Multiple replicas are running the same scheduler.
They coordinate using a quorum or lease.
One replica becomes leader for an epoch.
On failure, leadership moves while stale leaders are fenced.
leader-election.engineering: Use fencing tokens and lease expiry; a lock alone is not always sufficient for correctness.

backpressure.description: A slow consumer should not buffer messages indefinitely during a traffic surge.
steps: The producer emits requests faster than they are processed.
The queue starts filling toward its capacity.
The consumer requests only what it can safely process.
The system slows, sheds, or queues extra work according to policy.
backpressure.engineering: Reactive Streams request(n) supports demand; blocking operations still need appropriate schedulers.

threads-vs-webflux.description: Compare thread-per-request blocking I/O with non-blocking event-loop-based processing.
steps: A request needs to fetch downstream data.
A blocking thread waits during socket I/O.
Non-blocking WebFlux releases execution capacity while I/O is pending.
On completion, the response pipeline resumes.
threads-vs-webflux.engineering: WebFlux helps I/O-bound concurrency, not CPU-bound work; never block Netty event loops.

api-gateway.description: A single gateway authenticates requests before routing to order and catalog services.
steps: The app sends a request to a common public endpoint.
The gateway validates authentication and rate limits.
It routes the request to the correct service.
The response returns through the gateway.
api-gateway.engineering: Keep gateway logic thin; avoid turning it into a distributed monolith.

microservices-tradeoffs.description: Separate catalog and order services only when teams and scaling needs justify distributed complexity.
steps: A user places an order that references a product.
The order service validates domain rules.
Services exchange data through APIs or events.
Cross-service failures require retries and eventual consistency design.
microservices-tradeoffs.engineering: Service boundaries follow business ownership; distributed transactions and debugging cost real time.

url-shortener.description: Generate a unique short code and redirect visitors to the stored destination.
steps: A user submits a long URL to the API.
A unique token is generated and stored.
A visitor requests /abc123.
The service looks up the target and returns an HTTP redirect.
url-shortener.engineering: Consider collision handling, hot-link caching, abuse protection, and 301 versus 302 semantics.

chat-system.description: A WebSocket gateway delivers messages and stores them for offline recipients.
steps: A sender opens a persistent WebSocket connection.
A message is validated and given an ID.
The system persists it before delivery.
The recipient receives it or catches up after reconnecting.
chat-system.engineering: Ordering is usually per conversation; plan fan-out, reconnects, acknowledgments, and deduplication.

payment-system.description: Idempotency ensures a client retry does not create two charges for one order.
steps: Checkout submits a payment request with an idempotency key.
The service checks whether that key has already been processed.
The provider authorizes or declines the payment.
A verified webhook reconciles final state before fulfilment.
payment-system.engineering: Use durable idempotency records, signed webhooks, and explicit state transitions rather than naive retries.
